name: aegis (rust-aegis)
workload: AEAD encryption throughput chart at 16 KB messages (separate 64 KB chart for MAC-only)
claimed_speedup: On AMD Zen 4 (turbo disabled): AEGIS128L 208.44 Gb/s vs AES-128-GCM(BoringSSL) 50.83 Gb/s (~4.1x) and vs AES-256-GCM(BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s (~4.4x); AEGIS128X4 521.36 Gb/s (~10.9x vs AES-256-GCM/BoringSSL) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang recommended over gcc; CC="clang -O3 -march=native"; cargo bench / cargo-zigbuild bench; BoringSSL included via --features boring
hardware: AMD Zen 4 (turbo boost disabled); also charted on Apple M1 (MacBook Pro)
tradeoffs: AEGIS is a newer, non-NIST AES-based AEAD (CAESAR/IETF draft); needs AES-NI/ARM crypto extensions for its speed, falling back to a bundled softaes implementation otherwise; the crate vendors the C libaegis sources internally
caveats: Exact numbers are embedded only as a PNG chart in the README (read off the chart here, not machine-parsed text); comparison target is BoringSSL, not OpenSSL directly, so baseline_in_list=false; the vendored C backend derives from the separately-excluded aegis-aead/libaegis project

verification.tier_reason: The README chart compares against BoringSSL AES-128/256-GCM. The harness is public (benches/benchmark.rs, BoringSSL behind --features boring), the build is stated (CC="clang -O3 -march=native"; build.rs forces clang at -O3), and the CPUs are AMD Zen 4 (microarchitecture only) and Apple M1. That would be tier A, but the record duplicates libaegis.
verification.notes: Reject as a duplicate of aegis-aead/libaegis, which the catalogue already lists. rust-aegis is Rust bindings that bundle and compile libaegis's C code by default. It also has an independent pure-Rust backend, but that backend is slower and is not benchmarked. The numbers are not its own: the README chart is byte-identical (SHA-1 a76fffb3) to the libaegis README chart, which libaegis says is 'derived from libaegis'. The chart's Rust-crate labels suggest rust-aegis's cargo bench produced it, but it still measures the libaegis C code, and libaegis's catalogue entry already cites the same 208 vs 47.7 Gb/s figure.

name: stb_zip (CRC32 routine)
workload: CRC32 checksum of a 1GB in-memory buffer
claimed_speedup: CRC32 of 1GB data: 0.2 sec (stb_zip) vs 1.1 sec (miniz 3.0) = 5.5x
tradeoffs: Header-only single-file C library; only supports store/deflate ZIP entries, not a general-purpose zlib replacement.
caveats: First-party single-table README benchmark; miniz is a widely-used lightweight zlib-compatible library but is not the canonical zlib CRC32 baseline itself, and compiler/flags are unstated.
found_via: Independent benchmark suites and blogs (shootouts; harvest their winners): HN Algolia search "crc32 zlib"

verification.tier_reason: The README's BENCHMARKS table (Core i7-12700K, 32GB RAM) states 'CRC32 of 1GB data | 0.2 sec | 1.1 sec | 5.5x' vs miniz 3.0. The repo has only README.txt, LICENSE and stb_zip.h: no benchmark code, compiler or flags, so these are numbers without methodology.
verification.notes: The README numbers exist but belong to a different checksum. The only fast path computes CRC-32C, which is wrong for ZIP. The IEEE CRC-32 path matches miniz's byte-table algorithm, so the project is not actually faster at the baseline's function. It is also only 8 stars with 4 commits, all on 2025-08-13. Metadata checked: MIT, not a fork, not archived, stale (last commit 2025-08-13).
verification.reject_reason: Invalid evidence: the 5.5x fast path computes CRC-32C instead of the IEEE CRC-32 that ZIP requires (breaking its own ZIP CRC check); the correct IEEE path is the same byte-table algorithm as miniz's mz_crc32. No benchmark code.
